# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.instead: Besides the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult, who has to agree before they buy (a spouse, a family member, an audiologist)? "Nobody" is an answer.

screens.why1: Right after I said nobody else has to agree, it makes sense to show me the list Keel built so I can check it before strangers see it.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use myself: the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult has the problem and decides to buy, and nobody else is involved; the title repeated in the intro is only a small stutter.
screens.why3: I know exactly who buys AirCaps: the wearer orders and pays, HSA/FSA included, so this is my own knowledge.
screens.why4: The wearer appears twice, once as 'has the problem' and once as 'decides to buy', and 'Nobody else' carries no tag, so two rows overlap where one would do.
screens.why5: It still says what I picked: the wearer decides and pays and nobody else has to agree, with no role added.
screens.why7: The card says the person with the problem and the decider are one row when they are the same person, but here they are split into two, and 'Nobody else' is untagged; the belief (nobody else must agree) still matches my answer and the item can support or refute it.
screens.instead: The people involved. Keel used only the roles you named. Rows: Nobody else · does not have to agree; Deaf or hard-of-hearing adult · has the problem and decides to buy.

screens.why1: I just said nobody else has to agree, so it makes sense to confirm that as the belief before moving on, with a way back if I want to name someone.
screens.why2: The belief is plain, but the bar's 'paid for something for this' needs a second read (I'd say 'something like this'), and the two-sentence title is long for a confirm step.
screens.why3: I know my wearers mostly buy for themselves (HSA/FSA, $599 glasses), so whether they decide alone is something I can judge.
screens.why4: The list holds only Nobody else, which is what I picked, so as the card says it is a statement to confirm; it adds no role I never named, and the go-back route covers the case where I want to add one.
screens.why5: It says what I typed: the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides and nobody else has to agree, with no role invented or dropped.
screens.why7: With Nobody else tested, the bar counts only decided-alone as support, consistent with the card's 1-for, 3-against balance; the belief matches my list, and the stranger's item carries the I can't say escape.
screens.instead: Keep the screen, but word the bar: Holds if at least 2 in 3 deaf or hard-of-hearing adults say they decided on their own the last time they paid for something like this.

screens.why1: After who decides and who agrees, asking what first step I want my wearers to take before paying is the obvious next commercial question.
screens.why2: The question asks two things at once (the step and what it costs them), and the hint's examples, 'pay for a pilot' and 'let us run a trial', are B2B words that don't fit someone ordering glasses for themselves, so I'd read it twice before typing 'order the caption glasses with free returns'.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I want a hard-of-hearing adult to do first: order a pair on our 15-day risk-free returns, so I can answer straight from my own funnel.
screens.why4: The only option is the 'I'm not sure' chip, which the card allows on the founder side and which fits a founder who hasn't settled the first step.
screens.why5: My typed step stays verbatim, keeping 'caption glasses' and 'free returns', the terms that define what the person agrees to.
screens.why7: The box asks for the card's one step: up to 9 words, in the people's words, saying where any money goes, with the smaller free step promised on the next screen only when it costs money, data or a signature, and 'I'm not sure' as the founder's allowed out.
screens.instead: What's the first step you'd want deaf or hard-of-hearing adults to take, in up to 9 words? (e.g. "order a pair with free returns" or "try the free app first"; if it costs them money, data or a signature, Keel drafts a smaller free step next)

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first step, this is where I'd expect Keel to show me how strangers will hear it and what it will test.
screens.why2: The strangers' list reads cleanly, but the line 'Or a smaller step first: Yes, after Try a working pair of caption glasses first' is garbled, with a stray 'Yes, after' and a capital 'Try', so I had to read it twice to see it was the smaller step.
screens.why3: Ordering glasses with our 15-day returns is a real step my deaf and hard-of-hearing customers take on our site, and they know whether they would.
screens.why4: The four answers cover the range, but 'trying a working pair first' overlaps with the free-returns order, which is how most people try a pair today since we have no demo counters, so the soft yes is close to the firm yes.
screens.why5: 'Order the caption glasses with free returns' is my step word for word, the belief adds no timing or number, and no role leaks.
screens.why7: The first option is my step whole and the soft yes names a smaller free step, balanced 2 for and 2 against with no escape, but that smaller step largely repeats what free returns already gives (one rule bent), and the frame says '5 of 5' where the registry puts Commitment sixth.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you order the caption glasses with free returns, or not? Yes, I'd order the caption glasses with free returns · Probably, after a video call showing the captions live first · Probably not · No

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step, ordering the glasses with free returns, it makes sense to ask whether to collect the people who would actually take it.
screens.why2: A pilot and a yes/no choice are plain to me as a founder, and the hint says exactly what the respondent will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want emails from people ready to try the glasses is my own call and needs no guessing.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers the choice, the two options are distinct, and no escape is needed for a founder's own decision.
screens.why5: The hint's closing line is a generic 'Would you try this for real? Leave your email.' rather than the step I typed (order the caption glasses with free returns), so my commitment step drifts out of what respondents are offered.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would you order the caption glasses with free returns? Leave your email." — Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Picking the interviewer belongs just before launch, but for a study sent to deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, choosing a voice by how it sounds is the least important choice and feels off-key for my people.
screens.why2: Plain enough: two named voices, a five-second sample, a credit cost and a text-message link are all clear on first read.
screens.why3: I can hear both samples and choose, and I know my respondents will mostly read rather than listen.
screens.why4: Two voices are distinct, but for my audience the obvious missing option is a text-first or captioned-only interviewer (or a signing one), so a deaf respondent isn't greeted by a talking face they can't hear.
screens.why5: It keeps my 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults' wording and leaks nothing of AirCaps to the people answering.
screens.instead: How should Keel ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? -- Text on screen first, with the video muted by default / Video with live captions burned in (Daphne or Saskia voice) / Video voice only

screens.why1: After choosing who asks the questions, picking how my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents will answer is the natural last step before sending.
screens.why2: The question and the three options are plain to me, and Daphne was introduced on the screen before.
screens.why3: I know my wearers' communication well, and that is exactly what this asks me to weigh.
screens.why4: The options are distinct and complete for text versus AI, but the Daphne option leads with 'asks each question aloud' to a deaf audience, and nothing covers Deaf ASL users like the instructor who sees our glasses as one-directional.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is touched here, and my pick of Read and tap stands as typed.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? Read and tap (type or speak into boxes) / AI interviewer Daphne, every question captioned on screen as she speaks, answer by typing, tapping or talking / Let them choose.

screens.why1: Once the interviews are set up, the last thing to settle is who gets the link, so this belongs at the end of the flow.
screens.why2: The first and third options read plainly, but the second assumes I know what Keel's 'Contacts page' search is, and I have never seen it in this flow.
screens.why3: I know how I'd reach deaf and hard-of-hearing adults: people I know from the TranscribeGlass years by name, or a post in a community group, so I can answer this from my own life.
screens.why4: Named people, a list Keel found, and one open link for a group are three distinct routes that cover how I'd actually reach people, and my pick of 'people I know by name' is there.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is changed or leaked here; it is only about how links are sent.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name / A list Keel finds for me (on the Contacts page) / One open link I post in a group where they already are

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right under the title with its deciding number, Existing sacrifice at 1 of 7 losing 12 or more conversations a month, and the card shows that against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b2: Each card shows what is counted, out of 7, with the bar beside it, but the cards jump from 4 to 6 under a '5 beliefs' tally, so I looked twice for a missing card 5.
screens.why_b3: Price, Buyer and payer and Commitment are my words, but I put Existing sacrifice in dollars ($200 to $1,500 a year on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras), and here it is 'about 12 conversations a month', which I recognise but did not type as the money test.
screens.why_b4: The lines 'smaller than you think' and 'they value it below your price' tell me what failed, but nothing says what to do, such as testing a lower price or the free-caption tier first, even with 0 of 7 at $599.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and nothing is called strong, but the screen never says seven is a small sample, and 'they lose less today than you estimated' reads as a claim about deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in general.
screens.instead: Not holding up on money: none of the 7 would pay $599 up front or $20 a month, and only 1 of 7 loses 12 or more conversations a month; with only 7 people, try a lower glasses price or lead with the free plan before you trust this.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 1 of 7 at 12 or more against a bar of 5 of 7, and the two agree.
screens.why_b2: The count of people and the bar marker at 5 of 7 are plain, but the axis label 'conversations of the conversations they are in a month' forces a count through a share frame, and I had to read it twice to see the chart counts conversations per person.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Existing sacrifice and the belief is my count of about 12 conversations a month lost the thread of, in my own loss line.
screens.why_b4: The So line only says they put it below my estimate and hands me to the Price card; it never tells me what a lower cost means for selling $599 glasses or which number to revisit.
screens.why_b5: The small n is flagged as 'a lean, not a call'. But people were asked how many conversations 'fell through', while my belief is about conversations they lost the thread of, so 'they lose less than you estimated' rests on a narrower question than my belief.
screens.instead: Ask 'Last month, about how many conversations did you lose the thread of?', label the axis 'conversations per person last month', and say: most of these 7 lose 2 to 8, not 12 — lean the money case on the conversations that matter most rather than on how many.

screens.why_b1: Not holding up sits right beside 0 of 7 at $599 or more against a bar of 5 of 7, for both the up-front and the monthly step, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Both ladders show their counts per band with my $599 and $20 marked as band low edges, and each strip shows 7 cells all against with the marker at 5 of 7, so what is counted, over whom and where the bar sits are plain.
screens.why_b3: Price and $599 up front with an optional $20 a month plan are my actual pricing on the site, named as AirCaps, with nothing narrowed or dropped.
screens.why_b4: It tells me 6 of 7 put it at $250 to under $599 and sends me to Insights, but it does not say what that means for AirCaps, such as whether the gap is the glasses' sticker price or doubt they would work, which the try-first quotes point to.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 stays visible and it is called a small group, a lean, not a call; it claims nothing beyond those seven.
screens.instead: Say that 6 of 7 put the glasses at $250 to under $599, just under my $599, and that most who explained wanted to try a pair in their own hard setting first, so test whether a trial or the 15-day returns closes the gap before cutting the price; and since the plan is optional, say the monthly answers count apart from the glasses.

screens.why_b1: 'Not reached' sits right beside '0 of 7 named your price or more', and each person's row shows the band they named below $599, so I know why nothing was decided.
screens.why_b2: Three bars at 0 plus a strip of 5 ghost cells, when 7 people answered, take a second look; only the count line ('7 named less') tells me the chart is empty because nobody reached the question, and the 2-in-3 bar is never drawn.
screens.why_b3: The $599 up front and $20 a month plan are my prices, but I never typed a line about paying from money they already spend; Keel derived it, the card shows it as my belief, and the sentence ('who would pay ... could find it') reads awkwardly.
screens.why_b4: 'Ability to pay waits until at least 5 do' reads as if more answers would settle it, but all 7 answered below $599; the real next step is the price itself (the Price card), and this card doesn't point there.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the 7: n is visible, every person is listed as not asked, and no verdict is drawn from zero answers, though 'Only 0 of 7' is clumsy rather than misleading.
screens.instead: Not reached: none of the 7 named $599 or more up front (6 said $250 to under $599, 1 under $250), so nobody was asked where the money would come from. Settle the price first (see Price) before this question can be read.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 decided alone · bar 5 of 7', so I see both the verdict and the number that clears my bar in one line.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts who had to agree to their last such purchase over 7 people, with 6 for and 1 against, and the strip puts my bar plainly at 5 of 7 (at least 2 in 3).
screens.why_b3: 'Buyer and payer' and 'the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides, and nobody else must agree first' are what I picked: Nobody else, with the wearer paying.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the tally ('they decide alone; 1 of 7 needed someone's agreement'). It doesn't tell me to keep selling direct to the wearer, or that with the buyer settled the money problem is the price, not who signs.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (7 answered, 7 counted), the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing claims more than the six who decided alone.
screens.instead: Holding up, 6 of 7: the wearer buys alone, so keep selling straight to them (one needed a spouse's yes, so let a partner try them too); who signs isn't what's stopping you, the $599 is.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 said yes and bar 5 of 7, and the strip shows one against, well inside the 1-in-3 the bar allows.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts each of the four answers over the 7 who answered, and the strip puts the marker at 5 against 6 for, so what is counted, over whom and where the bar sits read on first look.
screens.why_b3: The belief and the asked question carry my step exactly, 'order the caption glasses with free returns', under the name Commitment, though the rule line's 'probably, after try a working pair' is a grammar slip I noticed.
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' fits a pilot better than a $599 pair of glasses, and it does not say concretely what to do with six people who said yes in principle.
screens.why_b5: The count line rightly calls it a lean, not a call, but the So line states flatly that 6 of 7 'would order' a hypothetical, after the Price card showed none of the same 7 valuing the glasses at $599, which overstates a soft yes.
screens.instead: Holding up, a lean: 6 of 7 said they'd order the caption glasses with free returns, though none put the price at $599. Send those six the order link with the 15-day returns and count who keeps them.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits directly beside '0 of 7 at $599 or more, once' and '0 of 7 at $20 or more a month' against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is Price and the belief line is word for word what I checked: $599 up front, then an optional $20 a month plan.
screens.why_b4: The groups hint at a direction (trial first, crowd pickup), but the screen never says what this means for the idea, and the 'When a line fails' header gives no concrete next step.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible (7 against, 6 asked, 1 never saw it, named), each quote carries that person's own price bands, and nothing is claimed beyond those six people.
screens.why_b6: I already offer 15-day free returns, yet two people still ask to borrow a pair first, so the returns offer is not reading as a trial. The quotes also show multi-speaker pickup (audience questions, eleven at lunch) as the thing that would raise the value, and that the monthly fee feels heavy next to free lip-reading.
screens.instead: Most of you landed at $250 to under $599 up front and under $10 a month; people want to try a pair before paying even though returns are free, so put a borrow or demo pair in front of the $599 ask and test a lower price.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it plainly checks whether I'm the kind of person the study is for, someone who deals with hearing people regularly.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is exactly how I and other deaf people say it, and 'every week' is clear on first read.
screens.why3: I know straight away: I talk with hearing people at work, in shops and at the theatre most weeks.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it with no overlap, and a gate rightly has no escape.
screens.why5: It matches the founder's segment of people who talk with hearing people every week, and nothing about any product leaks.
screens.why6: It's one short question that is easy to follow, though the spoken form should end with 'Yes or no.' as the guidelines say.

screens.why1: Right after checking I talk with hearing people every week, showing me the idea before asking about it makes obvious sense.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses, lens, eye contact: these are all words I use myself when I talk about following a conversation.
screens.why3: Looking down at a phone for captions and losing the person's face is something I deal with every week, so I can picture this from my own life.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options shown.
screens.why5: It reads as a plain description of a product, and nothing in it talks about me in a company's words or tells me who I am supposed to be.
screens.why6: It is sayable, but the second sentence repeats 'lightweight glasses with an app' and 'live captions inside the lens' straight after the first, which is tiring when heard, and 'when the people nearby are speaking, you wear' sounds like you only put them on when someone talks.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that shows live captions inside the lens. While people around you talk, you read what they say in the lens of your glasses. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and opening 'What you do today', asking how often conversations go wrong for me last month is an obvious place to start on what this already costs me.
screens.why2: 'Fell through' is not how I'd put it, since to me that means a plan got cancelled; I'd say a conversation I couldn't follow or lost track of, so I had to read it twice to guess what it meant.
screens.why3: I know which talks I lost the thread of, but counting them across a whole month means I'd be guessing a rough number, not recalling one.
screens.why4: A number box labelled 'conversations last month' with None and I can't recall covers every true answer I could give, and None is still served as 0.
screens.why5: The study is about a talk being too fast or too noisy to follow, and 'fell through' drifts from that into something like a conversation being called off.
screens.why6: Heard once it is short and one question, with the box and the one escape said plainly, though 'A number of conversations last month' is a little stiff.
screens.why7: The box counts conversations per month, which can be placed against the founder's low either way, but the item uses 'fell through', the vague verb the card says to avoid where the writer can name the thing I actually see go.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many conversations with hearing people couldn't you follow? [box] conversations last month · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: Asking what AirCaps would be worth makes sense right after the idea card, but the kicker still says "What you do today", and that jars on a question about a price for something I don't have yet.
screens.why2: "Up front" and "a month" are how I already think about buying hearing gear and paying for a caption app, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I've paid for hearing aids and tried caption apps, so I know what I'd put down for glasses and what I'd pay monthly to follow a conversation again.
screens.why4: The rungs are complete and don't overlap, and the escape fits, but "$250 to under $599" looks like a shop's sticker price stuck into my choices and stands out against the round numbers.
screens.why5: Only the idea card's own words reach me, AirCaps and captions in the lens, and nothing of the founder's plan or their names for people like me.
screens.why6: Each step says well and gives me four things to hold, but two ladders of two steps each make four rounds in a row, which is a lot by ear, and "five ninety-nine" is a fussy figure to hear.
screens.why7: Up front then a monthly plan gives two ladders of six, each with a band edge at the founder's low ($599, $20), bands below and above it, "I wouldn't pay for this" as an answer, and "I can't say" alone as the escape.
screens.instead: What would AirCaps be worth to you up front? Under $250 · $250 to under $600 · $600 to under $1,000 · $1,000 to under $2,500 · $2,500 or more · I wouldn't pay for this · I can't say -- with the kicker reading "About AirCaps", not "What you do today"

screens.why1: Right after I put a price on AirCaps, asking what would make it worth more is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: It reads back my answer the way I'd say it, about $250 to $600 up front, and the question is plain.
screens.why3: I know what would make it worth more to me, like keeping up in a noisy restaurant or a fast group conversation, so I can answer from my own week.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: AirCaps was named on the idea card, so using its name here leaks nothing new, and it stays on what the price question asked.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and the dollar amounts say cleanly with no symbol or parenthesis to trip on.

screens.why1: Right after asking what AirCaps would be worth to me, it makes sense to ask whether I could just buy it myself or whether somebody else had a say, like with my hearing aids.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use myself; I'd get it on one read or one hearing.
screens.why3: I've paid for hearing aids and a captioning app, so I know whether my husband, an audiologist or insurance had a say.
screens.why4: The four cover me alone, one other person, several people, or someone else deciding (like insurance or vocational rehab), and I can't say sits apart.
screens.why5: Nothing about the product or the founder's own terms leaks; it just says something like this.
screens.why6: Short, one question, four short options I can hold, one escape said last; the shift to you decided on your own is natural when spoken.
screens.why7: Nobody else is tested in the past form, with the four fixed answers in order (alone, someone else, several, someone else's call) and I can't say as the one escape; only decided on my own supports it and the other three count against.

screens.why1: After the price and who has to agree, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually order the glasses, though the 'What you do today' label sits oddly on a what-if.
screens.why2: Ordering caption glasses with free returns is plain to me; I'd answer it the first time I read or heard it.
screens.why3: Whether I'd order a pair of caption glasses for myself is my own decision, and I know what I'd do.
screens.why4: The options run from a firm yes, to a yes once I've tried a working pair, to probably not, to no; they cover what I'd say and don't overlap.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's step whole (order the caption glasses, free returns), and nothing leaks beyond the idea card I was shown on purpose.
screens.why6: One short question and four options I can hold when heard; the first option is long but says easily.
screens.why7: The first option is the founder's step word for word, and the soft yes is a smaller free step (trying a working pair) that leads to that same order; the list has two answers for and two against, with No as the floor and no escape.
